Elbing
EL-bing
n. (the royal Prussian port, Polish Elbląg, Lutheran from 1523, whose gymnasium taught Poles, Germans and Scots together)
German Elbing, Polish Elbląg, from the Elbing river and the old Prussian settlement of Truso; founded by the Teutonic Order in 1237.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Elbing is one of the three great Hanseatic towns of royal Prussia, with Danzig and Thorn, which took the Reformation by their own civic authority while remaining subjects of a Catholic Polish king. Lutheran preaching began there in 1523 and the council carried the town over in the following years; the king conceded in practice what he could not prevent, and the Prussian towns kept their Lutheran establishment, their guilds and their German law throughout the commonwealth's existence. Elbing's own contribution was educational and mercantile. Its gymnasium, reorganised in 1535 and raised to an academic gymnasium in 1598, taught Latin, Greek, Hebrew and theology to the sons of the Prussian towns and to Poles and Scots; the Eastland Company of English merchants had its staple there from 1579, and a Scottish and English Protestant colony grew up in the town. Elbing and Thorn gave the Lutheran churches of the commonwealth their steadiest ministry, because theirs did not depend on a nobleman. The dictionary enters Elbing because a town council, a school and a trade were enough to keep a church for two centuries where a province of great patrons could not keep one for two generations.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a gymnasium as a place of exercise or a school; a staple as an established mart of trade; a guild as an incorporated society; and a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough.

expand to see more

GYMNASIUM, n. A place where athletic exercises are performed; a school; in Germany, a high school or academy.

STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; an established town of trade; the principal commodity of a place.

GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.

BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town; one who possesses a municipal right.

COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Modern Corruption

Royal Prussian port, Lutheran by council decision from 1523, whose academic gymnasium taught Poles, Germans and Scots and whose church outlasted the Polish Reformation.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the church that cannot survive a change of patron, which Elbing avoided by being owned by nobody. Its ministers were called and paid by a town council answerable to its own burghers, its school was endowed by the same body, and the Polish crown could remove neither. The result was a congregation that went on quietly for two hundred years doing what the apostle commends, that men “study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11), and the churches so established are described in one line: “so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Act 16:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a church's investment in its own school, which is how doctrine is handed to the next set of officers. The apostolic charge is to commit what has been heard “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and an academic gymnasium teaching Hebrew to merchants' sons is a literal obedience to it. The promise over the whole arrangement is the old one, that if you “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6), when he is old he will not depart from it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit in trust; Greek bebaioo (G950), to confirm, to make firm; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful.

expand to see more

Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to set before, to commit in trust; “the same commit thou to faithful men”, 2 Timothy 2:2.

Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “commit thou to faithful men”, 2 Timothy 2:2.

Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train, to instruct; “Train up a child in the way he should go”, Proverbs 22:6.

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, to make firm; “were the churches established in the faith”, Acts 16:5.

Greek philotimeomai (G5389) — to make it one's ambition; “study to be quiet, and to do your own business”, 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

Usage

"“the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the academic gymnasium of 1598."

"“study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — a Hanseatic church owned by its own burghers."

"“were the churches established in the faith” (Act 16:5) — two centuries of Lutheran ministry under a Catholic king."
